note: Severity is a property of WHAT WAS DETECTED, not of the reviewer's opinion of it. Two kinds of evidence, and they differ in authority. A rule that NAMES the defect class (`exact` — a credential literal, a SyntaxError) fixes severity outright: the class is not a matter of taste. A rule that only knows WHICH TOOL RAN (`floor`) can raise a reviewer's label and never lower it, because a lint proof attached to a serious claim must not downgrade the claim. Both directions are measured, not assumed: without `exact`, one syntax error came back critical in two passes and high in the third, on the same line; without `floor`, a critical claim proven by a lint command was downgraded to low.

rules.why: The cited line contains a live-key literal, so the credential is in the tree whether or not gitleaks ran. Measured: without this rule a text-based proof of the same key kept the reviewer's `medium` while the tool-based proofs were `critical`.

Measured: a syntax error was proved through a linter and came back critical in two passes and high in the third, on the same line. Once a SyntaxError is cited the class is unambiguous, so it is fixed at high — the value the compile rule already assigns.
A committed credential is an access grant. The tool knows a secret was found, not which kind, so this raises rather than settles.
eval/exec/shell execution of data is remote code execution by construction; it is high rather than critical because exploitability still depends on what reaches the sink.
Code that does not parse cannot run at all. It is not critical because it fails loudly rather than silently.
A type error is a real defect that still compiles in Python, so it ships and misbehaves later.
A failing test is evidence of broken behaviour, but the test itself can be wrong, so it is not raised to high on the tool's word alone.
Lint findings are style and idiom; they do not by themselves change behaviour. A linter quoting a SyntaxError is caught by `does-not-parse-literal`, which is exact.
Nix lint findings are idiom and anti-pattern warnings; the evaluator still accepts them.
An unused binding is dead code, not a defect in behaviour.
Shellcheck's findings are often unquoted expansions and swallowed errors, which change behaviour under real input.
